demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless she was also physically injured, which is not reflected elsewhere. The other selected appraisals center on self-blame and humiliation, which fit this trauma type, but this item introduces a different trauma meaning without supporting threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a broad, ongoing danger/vulnerability pattern focused on personal safety (restricted safe places, nighttime checking for safety). For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, this is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma involving danger to self; the threat content would more plausibly center on fear of causing harm again, moral threat, or social/legal consequences.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active edge is Threat → Negative Appraisals, so threat and appraisals should show a plausible thematic link. Here the threat items center on physical safety and hypervigilance, while the appraisals center on guilt, self-blame, and humiliation about having caused harm. That disconnect suggests the selected threat items are not well aligned with the appraisals for this trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the threat profile is poorly matched: nocturnal checking for safety and inability to relax in safe places imply an ongoing danger/victimization-based fear response, but the appraisals center on guilt and self-blame about causing harm. That combination is hard to reconcile clinically without any items about fear of legal retaliation, being attacked, or another external threat.

issues.item: Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Negative Appraisals, so threat items should plausibly feed the selected appraisals. Here the threat items suggest current physical danger/hypervigilance, whereas the negative appraisals are predominantly moral self-judgment and shame. Humiliation in particular is weakly connected to the stated threat content, making the cross-node pattern clinically incoherent.

vignette: Clara Vance was sixty-six when the heavy aluminum backdrop frame gave way during a commercial campaign shoot. She had been shifting the stand to diffuse the overhead keys, her own joints stiff from years of holding rigid angles under hot lights. When the crossbar slipped from her grip, it swung forward with a sharp, metallic crash. Clara lunged to catch it, but her heel caught the edge of a tape line. The frame collapsed onto the floor where a lighting assistant was kneeling to secure a cable. The steel bar struck his shoulder and ribs, and the studio dissolved into frantic shouts and the sound of the gurney being wheeled out. Clara stood frozen, her hands still extended, watching the paramedics lift the stretcher. She had moved the frame without checking the stabilizing clips. She had been standing too close. She had not held it steady enough to guide it down. In the weeks that followed, Clara returned to her Connecticut home, but safety never settled into her posture. Even when she sat in her sunlit parlor and knew the doors were locked, her shoulders remained braced, her breath stayed shallow, and her muscles coiled tight, as if waiting for another heavy object to fall. The memory did not unfold as a story she could examine; it returned as a sudden flash of steel and a sharp gasp whenever she heard the heavy thud of a door or the clatter of tools being set on tile. When her agency called to discuss a reduced schedule, she would lose her place mid-sentence, the words blurring before she could finish them. She was certain that anyone with proper training would have double-checked the frame, would have secured the base, would never have positioned themselves so recklessly. The shame of it settled over her like a heavy coat. She could not shake the image of her own hands failing to catch the bar, of her hesitation when the paramedics arrived, of the way she had stood by rather than directing the response. She had come to believe she would never pardon herself for standing still when seconds mattered. Over the following months, her routines narrowed. She canceled fittings with tailors who asked her to stand in cramped, mirrored dressing rooms, finding herself unable to tolerate the reflective surfaces that showed her own rigid posture. She stopped attending industry luncheons, excusing herself when the waitstaff began wheeling out carts with heavy glassware. The consequences accumulated quietly. Her stylist stopped leaving detailed scripts on her desk, knowing she could not retain the blocking notes. A longtime friend from the agency stopped calling, frustrated by the canceled plans and the way Clara would flinch whenever a chair scraped against tile. Clara did not blame them; she simply found that the world kept moving with a physicality she could no longer match. Her own body felt like a warning siren that refused to power down, scanning every threshold, every passing shadow, every sudden shift in the room. She would rehearse breathing exercises in her kitchen, yet the tension in her neck and shoulders refused to yield, leaving her exhausted by noon. The decision to seek help arrived not with a single moment, but with a slow erosion of what kept her grounded. She attempted to read her late husband’s old photography books, but the pages blurred into a uniform gray, and her mind kept returning to the weight of the frame in her hands. She called the clinic on a Tuesday morning, her voice steady but her knuckles white around the receiver. She wanted to understand why her body would not rest, why her memory kept replaying the collapse, why the mirror in her hallway felt like a judgment. She hoped, quietly, that someone might help her untangle the knot of her own responsibility without stripping away the reality of what she had caused. What frightened her most was the possibility that the tension in her frame and the silence in her days would never loosen, and that she would lose the last fragments of the life she had built before she ever found a way to let them go.
